name: Lena Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Ashby Orchards, about sixty hectares of apples and pears on the slopes above Westbrook. November is the end of picking, the late apples, then it's tidying the rows and, from December, winter pruning, which is the part I'm worst at. I start at half seven, there's six of us on the permanent crew, and Rui, the foreman, gives us our rows on a whiteboard in the shed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into orchard work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was the receptionist at Westbrook Primary for twenty-six years. Then they brought in an online system for absences and dinner money, and my hours were cut to mornings only, which didn't pay the bills. My neighbour picks at Ashby every autumn and said they were short of permanent staff, so three years ago I swapped a desk for a ladder. My knees weren't consulted.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love blossom week in April, honestly, the whole slope goes white and pink and the bees are deafening. What's hard is pruning, Rui can look at a tree and see next year's fruit, and I just see branches. And money, Imran, my husband, is a self-employed plumber, so some months are good and some aren't, and we've never had more than a few weeks put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds sensible, a useful tool and no drama. I use one of those chat things now and then myself, mostly when I'm writing a tricky letter. I'd say it at work and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, though I've seen what a handy tool can do. The online absence system was only a handy tool too, and it cut my job in half. So I'd be relieved but watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd maybe ask the chat thing to explain pruning, the bit about fruit buds versus leaf buds, because I'm too embarrassed to ask Rui again. And I'd keep the Christmas club going at the shop, ten a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. With one eye open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the online system at the school.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was sold to us as saving time on the phones. And it did. Parents tapped in absences instead of ringing me, and the head realised that meant she only needed me till twelve. Nobody was nasty about it, that's the thing, it just happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you actually used the chat tool for pruning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, on my break, behind the shed. It told me fruit buds are fatter and rounder than leaf buds, which Rui had told me twice, but somehow reading it slowly made it stick. I didn't tell anyone, they'd tease me.

S0.say: I'd say it sounds sensible, a useful tool with no drama. I use a chat tool now and then myself, mostly for tricky letters.
S0.think: I'd be relieved but watching, because the school's online absence system was only a handy tool too, and it cut my job in half.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and asks the chat tool to explain pruning so she doesn't have to ask the foreman again. Keeps paying ten a week into the Christmas club.
S0.feel: Mostly calm, with one eye open.
S0.quote: Nobody was nasty about it, that's the thing, it just happened.
S0.fieldNote: Lena has already lost half a job to a 'handy tool', so even the calmest picture makes her watchful. Her steady habit shows in quietly using AI to learn pruning in private. She's practical and slightly embarrassed about being slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to sort things out properly, if people are sensible. Schools and colleges should keep training young people, and companies should keep some beginner jobs even if they don't strictly need them. Middle of the road, that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is the picture where people like me just quietly lose hours, like I did at the school. Not sacked, just trimmed. That's how it would go at Ashby too, I think, a bit less winter work each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to make myself the one they keep. I'd ask Rui if I could shadow him on pruning for a week, properly, and practise on the old trees at the bottom of the hill. And I'd ask Imran to keep his bookings diary on the computer so we can see the lean months coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I recognise this one, that's what makes it uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you recognise it. Which part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The part where nobody decides anything. At the school there was never a meeting where they said Lena's going to part-time. It just drifted. That's what I'd be watching for at Ashby, the drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rui when you asked to shadow him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I know I'm slow, but I'm not stupid, and I'd rather learn from you than from a phone. He'd like that, Rui's proud of his trees. Then I'd probably still look it up on the phone at night.

S1.say: I'd say ten years is enough to sort things out if people are sensible. Schools should keep training young people and companies should keep some beginner jobs.
S1.think: This is the picture where people like me quietly lose hours rather than get sacked, like I did at the school. At Ashby it'd be a bit less winter work each year.
S1.do: Asks the foreman to let her shadow him pruning for a week and practises on old trees. Gets her husband to keep his bookings diary on the computer to spot lean months early.
S1.feel: Uneasy, because she recognises the slow drift from her school job.
S1.quote: I'd say, I know I'm slow, but I'm not stupid, and I'd rather learn from you than from a phone.
S1.fieldNote: She knows from experience that slow change arrives as drift, not decisions, and she'd be watching for it. Her plan was practical and steady: get better at the one skill that makes her worth keeping. Her line to Rui mixed honesty and charm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sad, and that both parties should stop point-scoring and agree a plan, retraining and some help with bills while people find their feet. I'd say it at the school gate when I pick up my grandson. People there would be worried, so I'd keep it calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thinking about my daughter Zara, who's a trainee accountant at a firm in the city. Routine office work is half of what she does at her level, she told me. And I'd think, I left the office just in time, which is a funny thing to feel lucky about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Zara and ask her straight what parts of her job she thinks could go. If it looked bad, I'd tell her to get her exams done fast, because qualified people seem to last longer than trainees. And I'd stop the Christmas club, ten a week, and keep it as a little emergency pot instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for Zara. For me, more of a strange relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think Zara would say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say Mum, everyone's using it already, we're fine. She always says we're fine. Then she'd ring back two days later at ten at night, which is how I know she's not fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you left the office just in time. Do you really feel lucky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucky's a strong word for a woman with bad knees up a ladder. But yes, a bit. Three years ago I thought I'd fallen down the ladder of life, and in your picture it turns out I climbed off just before it broke.

S2.say: I'd say it's sad and both parties should stop point-scoring and agree on retraining and help with bills. I'd keep it calm at the school gate.
S2.think: I'd be thinking of my daughter, a trainee accountant doing lots of routine office work. And I'd think I left the office just in time, which is a funny thing to feel lucky about.
S2.do: Rings her daughter to ask which parts of her job could go and urges her to finish her exams fast. Turns the ten-a-week Christmas club into an emergency pot.
S2.feel: Anxious for her daughter and strangely relieved for herself.
S2.quote: Three years ago I thought I'd fallen down the ladder of life, and in your picture it turns out I climbed off just before it broke.
S2.fieldNote: Her centre instinct shows in calls for both sides to agree a plan. The private side was a mix of fear for her daughter and an unexpected relief at having left office work. The ladder image was lovely and very her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared fairly, some tax on the big winners, some help for those who lost out, but nothing crazy. Somebody has to calm it down. I'd say that to anyone, and I'd vote for whoever sounded calmest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a mixed bag. The orchard's fine, physical work is safe. But Imran fixes boilers and bathrooms for office people, and if lots of them lose their jobs, nobody books a new bathroom. And Zara could be out, and she'd come home to us, with her student loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Rui for every hour going, including Saturday grading in the packhouse, which pays a bit more. Imran would chase his unpaid invoices hard, there's always two or three. And I'd clear out Zara's old room, quietly, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like the ground moving under the house while the house itself looks fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Clearing out Zara's room. Would you tell her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd tell her I was having a sort-out. She'd see through it, she's an accountant, she sees through everything. But it would make me feel better to have it ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: House prices are booming in this picture. Do you own your home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got a mortgage with eleven years left, which in your picture means our house is worth more on paper. Lovely, but you can't eat a valuation. If Imran's work dried up, we'd struggle to pay the mortgage on a house that's suddenly worth a fortune.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should be shared fairly, with some tax on big winners and help for those who lost out, but nothing crazy. I'd vote for whoever sounded calmest.
S3.think: The orchard's fine, but my husband fixes bathrooms for office people, and if they lose jobs nobody books one. And my daughter could lose her job and move home.
S3.do: Asks the foreman for every hour going, including Saturday packhouse grading. Gets her husband to chase unpaid invoices hard and quietly clears out her daughter's old room just in case.
S3.feel: Anxious, like the ground moving under the house while the house looks fine.
S3.quote: Lovely, but you can't eat a valuation.
S3.fieldNote: The squeeze reached her through her husband's plumbing work and her daughter's job, not the orchard. She was sharp on the paradox of a house worth more while the mortgage gets harder. Clearing the room quietly showed how she prepares without alarming anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper plan for older workers, not just a speech. Phase it in, give people notice, pay for training, and have some sort of bridge to the pension. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it would be me first. There's already a picking machine on trial at a big orchard down the valley, with suction tubes that take the apple off the branch, Rui went to see it. If they get one that prunes too, the woman who can't tell a fruit bud from a leaf bud doesn't stand a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Rui to put me forward to work alongside whatever machine comes, loading it, checking it, cleaning it. I'd do a course if there was one, I'd ask the chat thing which ones are any good. And at home, we'd cut the second phone contract and the streaming, about forty a month, and I'd ask Imran to look for steady work with the council instead of self-employed jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That sinking feeling of losing a job the slow way, but this time fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz, who's sixty-one and has pruned these trees for thirty years. He's brilliant and he won't touch a phone. If they keep anyone, it should be him, but he's the one who'd refuse to work with the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask the chat thing for courses. Is that new for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I use it now and then, not every day. But I've noticed I reach for it more when I'm frightened. Like a nightlight.

S4.say: I'd say we need a proper plan for older workers, phased in, with notice, training and a bridge to the pension. I'd say it calmly but more than once.
S4.think: I think it would be me first. A picking machine is already on trial down the valley, and if one prunes too, the woman who can't tell a fruit bud from a leaf bud doesn't stand a chance.
S4.do: Asks the foreman to put her forward to work alongside the machine, loading, checking and cleaning it, and uses the chat tool to find a course. Cuts about forty a month from phones and streaming and pushes her husband to seek steady council work.
S4.feel: Alarmed, with the sinking feeling of losing a job the slow way, only fast.
S4.quote: I've noticed I reach for it more when I'm frightened. Like a nightlight.
S4.fieldNote: She was frank that her weak pruning makes her first in line. Her plan was steady rather than bold: stand next to the machine and make herself useful. The nightlight image showed how her use of AI grows with fear, and she worried most for a skilled older colleague who won't adapt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, because the others happen to my family and that one happens to me and my family at once. What would help is notice, a year at least, and something that carries people in their late fifties to the pension without losing the house. I don't need a new career. I need seven years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the trees. Some of ours are forty years old, and Rui says a machine would want them all ripped out and replanted in straight lines it can reach. I'd miss the old ones. Silly, maybe.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I wish someone had asked the school receptionist before they brought in that system. Ask the people doing the job first. That's all.

headlineQuote: Three years ago I thought I'd fallen down the ladder of life, and in your picture it turns out I climbed off just before it broke.
portrait: Lena Khan is 58, a former primary school receptionist whose hours were halved by an online system, who has worked for three years on the permanent crew at a sixty-hectare apple and pear orchard. Her husband Imran is a self-employed plumber, they have a few weeks of savings and a mortgage, and she uses a chat tool now and then, more when she's frightened. She reads the early pictures through the slow drift that cost her the school job, worries next for her trainee accountant daughter and her husband's bookings, and feels an odd relief at having left office work. In the robot picture she expects her weak pruning to make her the first to go, and hopes to work alongside the machines.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because it hits her own job and her family at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: At least a year's notice and something to carry people in their late fifties to the pension without losing their home. She'd also want workers asked first before new systems arrive.
